title: Development of Acute Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy 11 Days after Spinal Surgery: A Case Report and Literature Review
case_prompt: An 81-year-old Japanese woman presented with a 1-year history of neurogenic claudication and bilateral thigh pain from lumbar stenosis (L1–5) with L4/5 spondylolisthesis. She underwent an uncomplicated L1–5 laminectomy with L4/5 posterolateral fusion. She ambulated with a walker and had no acute issues until postoperative day 9, when she had a single episode of soft stool without systemic symptoms. On day 11, she experienced sudden severe bilateral thigh pain, followed by ascending weakness and worsening tingling in both lower extremities. She was afebrile, alert, and without cranial nerve deficits. Examination showed 4/5 strength in the upper distal extremities, 3/5 strength throughout the lower extremities, hyperesthesia of the distal lower legs, preserved upper-limb reflexes, and absent patellar and Achilles reflexes. Routine blood tests were normal. Serum anti-GM1-IgG and anti-GalNAc-GD1a-IgG antibodies were positive (optical densities 0.157 and 0.135). Spinal CT and MRI showed no cord compression, epidural hematoma, abscess, implant displacement, or nerve-root compression; brain MRI was normal. An acute polyradiculoneuropathy was suspected, and a nerve conduction study was planned.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Mechanical compression (hematoma, implant displacement, recurrent herniation) was unlikely — “Spinal computed tomography showed no evidence of spinal cord compression…”  
2. Epidural hematoma or abscess was excluded — “MRI … without an epidural hematoma or abscess.”  
3. Spinal cord or nerve-root ischemia or injury was considered but imaging revealed no cord or root compression — “MRI of the whole spine showed … without significant cord or nerve root compression.”  
4. Infectious or inflammatory surgical-site complications were unlikely given the absence of fever and normal blood tests — “She was conscious and afebrile, and her surgical wound was healing well.”  
5. Acute polyradiculoneuropathy (GBS) was suspected based on the clinical triad of ascending weakness, sensory disturbance, and areflexia without mechanical causes — “An acute polyradiculoneuropathy was suspected based on rapidly progressive ascending weakness, sensory disturbance, and areflexia of the lower extremities without implant-related complications.”  
6. AIDP was favored over nodopathy because NCS showed temporal dispersion without conduction block on follow-up — “the findings of temporal dispersion … and no evidence of conduction block support the diagnosis of AIDP rather than nodopathy.”  
7. AIDP was distinguished from AMSAN by the characteristic sensory pattern of an abnormal median and normal sural response — “Abnormal median and normal sural sensory responses are highly suggestive of acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy …”
